title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known. Findings go to the searched log, unanswered questions to the open questions, errors to the corrections, and letters to the errands — but what this archive was actually going to do next lived only in a chat window, which is the one place that does not survive.
lead:
Every other register on this site answers *«what do we know?»*. This one answers *«what is being done?»*, and it exists because that question was being carried in a conversation, and a conversation is not a record.

**Five states.** *Running* means somebody or something is at it now. *Next* means it is ready to start. *Blocked* means it is waiting on a person or an institution, and the [errands](/errands/) carry the letter or the fee. *Done* means finished and published. *Struck* is for an item founded on a mistake — **kept and ruled through rather than deleted**, which is how this archive treats a retracted claim everywhere else.

**Every item names who has to move it.** An item with no owner is how a list becomes wallpaper, and the estate board sorts on that field, so the question it answers is *«what is waiting on me?»*

rows.what: Keep this archive's work list in the estate's shape, with the build refusing when it slips
rows.note: Written first in the **Defranceschi** archive and now in the shared kit, so eight archives keep one list in one shape instead of eight sessions each inventing one. The kit pin moved from `b16bea7` to **`60aad58`** to pick up `WorkList.astro` and `checkworklist.py`, and `check:worklist` now sits beside `check:kit` and `check:living` in the build. It is the gate, not the good intention, that makes a convention hold here — the same reason the menu canon and the [living-person rule](/method/) held when four written-down conventions drifted.

rows.what: Fold Porter, Jeayes, the Army Lists and the Royal Military Calendar into the register pages
rows.note: **Done.** [Sources](/sources/) now carries a table of the **fourteen printed and catalogued sources this archive has actually opened** — Porter both volumes, the Army Lists, the Royal Military Calendar, Connolly, the Gazette, Smyth's Description and Lives, Jeayes, Rudder, Bigland, the 1608 muster, Gloucestershire Notes & Queries and Discovery — each with the edition read, where it is free, and what it gave. Two are listed for what they did **not** contain, and one for an error it found here.

rows.what: Rewrite the coverage verdicts for the six indexes controlled this week
rows.note: **Done — eleven rows added and the optimistic verdicts replaced.** [Coverage](/coverage/) now runs to 50 rows and records what was measured rather than assumed: FreeREG's Berkeley is **1653–1677** and neither Awre nor Blakeney is in it at all; **FreeBMD silently refuses a wide date range**; the Gazette gazetted no engineer commission in 1774, 1775 or 1776; the Protestation Returns skip Gloucestershire; the 1381 poll tax skips Berkeley hundred; and Discovery and the Berkeley Castle catalogue are free, open and rich.

rows.what: Generate the open questions instead of hand-writing them
rows.note: **Done. 405 lines of prose became 81 lines and a data file.** [Open questions](/open-questions/) is generated from `questions.json` — **five open, three blocked, three closed and kept** — and every question now names what would settle it, which register holds the attempts, and the date it was raised, with anything over thirty days marked. It carries this week's work because it cannot help carrying it.

rows.what: Give the errands a state field of their own
rows.note: **Done.** Every errand now carries a `state` — **50 open, 8 answered and kept** — rendered as a tally at the head of the queue and a coloured rule on each row, so the count is a number instead of a reading exercise. Answered errands are kept rather than deleted, the same way a struck work-list item is.

rows.what: Name the control behind every null in the searched log
rows.note: **Done, and the number is worse than I guessed.** Of 89 null and empty rows, **30 name a control and 59 do not** — I had estimated forty. Rather than invent controls for rows searched weeks ago, each now carries its state on the page: «control named» in grey, «no control stated» in red. An unstated control does not make a row wrong, it makes it untested, and the page now says so instead of letting them all look equally solid.

rows.what: Read the archive against itself again once the consolidation lands
rows.note: **Done, and it found nothing real — which is the right answer this time.** 256 files and pages, 127 dated pairs, **31 flagged**. The one with the dangerous shape — Joseph D'Arcy baptised, 1779 in three files against 1780 in eleven, a spread of one — turns out to be the documented «adjacent events» false positive: the 1779 is **Robert and Jean's marriage**, sitting within seventy characters of the 1780 baptism. The other thirty are repeated forenames across generations. Last run it found six stale 1778s; this run the archive agrees with itself.

rows.what: Porter's History of the Corps of Royal Engineers, volume 2
rows.note: **Done, and it is the wrong volume — which is itself the answer.** Read in full text, free: neither D'Arcy appears in 1.5 million characters. Controlled by subject, not by name — the volume mentions the Peninsula 48 times, Waterloo 11 and **the Crimea 43**. It is Porter's post-1815 volume; Robert D'Arcy's service ran 1776 to about 1809, which is volume 1, already read. Joseph was Royal **Artillery**, so no volume of Porter was ever going to hold him.

rows.what: Smyth of Nibley, Lives of the Berkeleys, volume 2
rows.note: **Done, and redirected to volume 3, which is where the Swonhunger material actually is.** The Berkeley Castle catalogue cites «Transcript: Smyth, iii. 380-1» for the 1356 inspeximus. Volume 3 — the Description of the Hundred — gives 49 mentions of Swonhunger, **three further alias statements** beyond the one this archive had been quoting, and a named freehold, **Oldminster**, that can be followed from Smyth's survey of about 1639 into a Gloucestershire deed of 1690–1741. [Written up](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: Gloucestershire Notes & Queries, and the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society transactions
rows.note: **Done, and it found an error in this archive rather than a new ancestor.** Gloucestershire Notes & Queries reviewed Maclean's 1902 edition of the 1608 muster — the edition /saniger-1608 is built from — and listed its misreadings, including «**Sainger should read Saniger**». The man living in the hamlet is **John Saniger of Saniger**, his name and his address the same word, and the muster holds **three** spellings in 1608, not four. Now [correction 31](/what-we-got-wrong/). Three further volumes gave a clean null against a Berkeley control. TBGAS remains: forty volumes are digitised and unread.

rows.what: Rudder and Bigland — the two standard Gloucestershire county histories
rows.note: **Done, and the null was the finding.** Rudder (1779) does not name Saniger anywhere in 5.7 million characters — and his index *does* carry Wanswell, Hamfallow, Halmore and Alkington, so the control holds. At page 280 he gives the whole tithing as «Hamfallow, in which are Wanſwell… part of Halmore; and Hamfallow». **Smyth names it in 1639, Rudder omits it in 1779, Bigland names it in 1791** — and they put it in different tithings, which is what happens to a hamlet on a boundary. The same paragraph gave the **Thorps of Wanswell** a named tower at Berkeley Castle and carried the estate to 1525.

rows.what: FreeBMD again, this time with a control that can fail
rows.note: **Done, and the control earned its keep twice over.** FreeBMD **silently refuses** a wide date range and redisplays its own form — indistinguishable from an empty result, and three searches were recorded as nought before the control showed they had never run. Charlotte Darcy, 1869, came back «Brighton 2b 152», matching what this archive already held. Narrowed to 1850–52, SANIGAR returns **John (Mar 1850, Thornbury 11/401), Lydia (Sep 1851, 11/329) and Mary Ann (Dec 1851, 11/369)** — the same three deaths this archive had from the *local* register, now with GRO references to order against.

rows.what: FreeREG for the Gloucestershire parishes around Awre, at parish level
rows.note: **Done, and the parish-level control changed the answer.** SMITH in Berkeley returns 3 exact and 36 uncertain, **every one between 1653 and 1677** — so FreeREG's Berkeley holding is a thirty-year seventeenth-century fragment, not a register run. SANIGER there returns **0 exact**: a real null, but only thirty years wide. And the place list settles the Forest parishes outright — FreeREG has 189 Gloucestershire places and **neither Awre nor Blakeney is one of them**.

rows.what: The Gloucestershire Archives online catalogue, for Saniger and Swonhunger
rows.note: **Done, and the shape of the answer matters more than the count.** 127 unique records across six spellings, 33 at Gloucestershire Archives, 1601 to the 1990s. Seven new — and six of those seven are deeds in which **Saniger is the land, not the party**: Abevan, Hathway, Morse, Smith, Plomer and Vizard all holding «at Saniger». The catalogue independently confirms Bigland and Smyth: a hamlet far more people lived in than were named for.

rows.what: Three PROB 11 wills, digitised and free, behind a free sign-in this archive will not make
rows.note: **Elizabeth Saniger 1833**, **Robert D'Arcy**, and **Benjamin Cotton, cordwainer of Berkeley, 1779** (PROB 11/1056/294). All three are already digitised at Kew and cost nothing to download — the only obstacle is the account, and creating accounts is not something this archive does on your behalf. Cotton's will is the one that would test whether Catherine Cotton, who married Thomas Saniger at Berkeley, is his daughter.

rows.what: Two certificates to order, both against references already in hand
rows.note: **Lydia Sanigar's**, about £12.50 from the GRO against register 3 entry 265 — she was invisible under SANIGER and found only under the misspelling. And **the marriage of James Sneyd and Ann Biddulph**, Stoke St Peter 1842, ordered locally from Stoke-on-Trent against reference 31/03/214 rather than from the GRO. The marriage certificate would name **both fathers and their trades**, carrying the Sneyd line back a generation on a side this archive has never had.

rows.what: The letter to the Gloucestershire Family History Society, drafted and unsent
rows.note: Gloucestershire Archives replied on 14 September and named the Society's volunteers as the route they recommend, since they offer no research service themselves. The draft is written and sitting in `notes/letters/`. **Mail from your address is your call to send**, so it stays here until you do.

rows.what: Every index that wants an account or a bot check stays unread
rows.note: Ancestry, ScotlandsPeople, RootsIreland, FamilySearch, Geneanet, RootsChat and Archive.org's lending library all want an account; irishgenealogy.ie and British History Online put a bot check in the way. **This archive creates no accounts and solves no CAPTCHAs**, so these are recorded as `blocked` rather than as nulls — the distinction matters, because a blocked source has not said no, it has not been asked. [Behind the paywall](/behind-the-paywall/) lists what each would cost.

rows.what: England first — the Australian and Italian side deliberately set down
rows.note: A standing instruction, recorded here so it does not read as neglect: **keep digging at the English ancestry, not Brisbane and not the Falco side.** NSW BDM, the Antenati, BillionGraves and the Queensland indexes are deprioritised by decision, not by oversight. The Falco material has [its own archive](/the-other-archives/).

rows.what: Carry 1778 as the date of Robert D'Arcy's first commission
rows.note: Wrong, and wrong on six pages at once. The printed Army List of 1781 interleaves each engineer with his seniority date and puts him in a ditto-chain reading **17 January 1776**; the 1778 list carries the same run and Connolly agrees on the year. The page that was wrong was the one that sounded most authoritative — it named a record series and claimed a superlative. Kept here ruled through, as [correction 29](/corrections/).

rows.what: Treat FreeCEN's silence on the Sussex sisters as a null
rows.note: Justified at the time by SMITH in Sussex returning **1,000** — which is FreeCEN's display cap, so the number could not have gone higher whether the county were half-transcribed or whole. **A control that cannot fail is not a control.** The surname ARCY returns nought in Sussex 1851 while this archive has the three sisters in that very census at HO107/1646 f.357: the piece simply is not in FreeCEN. The row is now an `empty`, not a `null`. [Correction 30](/corrections/).

rows.what: Two archives in the estate still keep no work list
rows.owner: the Luwinski and Our Family sessions
rows.note: Raised here because it belongs to other archives and would otherwise go unsaid. Running the gate across the whole estate — `checkworklist.py --root . --all` — reports **8 archives, 153 rows, 113 open, and two with no list at all**: Luwinski and Our Family. Until those exist, the estate board is a board of six. The **Defranceschi** archive wrote this register first and the estate took it up; the shared version then added `owner` and `since`, and that session had already brought its twenty rows into line before this one was written.

rows.what: Sweep the National Archives' Discovery catalogue for all three surnames
rows.note: **Done, and it was the biggest single return of the week.** Searching Discovery is free and needs no sign-in. The catalogue had been searched on 14 September under **Saniger** and gave 71 records; searched today under the spellings the medieval clerks actually used it gives **195 unique records across thirteen forms** — 178 at Berkeley Castle, and the rest at Gloucestershire, Kew, Birmingham, Bristol, Hertford and Aberystwyth. Seventeen of the twenty-five read closely were new. Written up at [the name in its own century](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: The Gloucestershire Protestation Returns of 1641–42, where they survive
rows.note: **Done, and the answer is that they do not survive — proved rather than assumed.** The returns are one alphabetical series of county bundles at the Parliamentary Archives, YHL/PO/JO/10/1/77 to /109. Listing every bundle shows Essex, Hampshire, Hertfordshire and Huntingdonshire sharing a single piece, and **Gloucestershire absent from a run that passes straight through where it belongs**. The alphabet is the control and it could have failed. Staffordshire, for the Sneyds, does survive.

rows.what: The Gloucestershire hearth tax returns of 1671–72
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question; the reading is now an errand.** A 1671–72 Gloucestershire hearth tax survives twice — Gloucestershire Archives **D383/1** (photostat of the enrolment, with a part transcript) and Kew **E 179/329** (400 folios, «includes names of individuals»). Neither is digitised. The better find was **D5555/2/9**, one bundle transcribing *Men and Armour* 1608, the hearth taxes of 1664 and 1672 and the poll tax of 1678. And a null worth as much: the 1381 poll tax photostats list every surviving membrane, and **Berkeley hundred is not among them**.

rows.what: The Berkeley Castle Muniments catalogue, not just Jeayes's 1892 calendar
rows.note: **Done, and it did not need a letter.** The Berkeley Castle Muniments are catalogued item by item inside Discovery — party, land, rent, witnesses and the GC number to quote when requesting the document — so the modern catalogue this archive wanted turns out to be free and already open. **178 records** under the medieval spellings. Errand 51 asked for exactly this and can be closed.

rows.what: The London Gazette, read end to end for both D'Arcys
rows.note: **Done, and the null turned out to be structural.** Neither D'Arcy appears in the Gazette 1770–1830; all twenty-two Darcy notices of 1770–89 are other men. Controlled first — the decade carries 1,057 «Lieutenant» notices — and then explained: the Ordnance gazetted **no** British engineer commissions in 1774, 1775 or 1776, began during the American war and was routine by the mid-1780s. It also dated something the archive was vague about: the Corps of Engineers became the **Royal** Engineers by warrant on 23 April 1787. [The Corps](/the-corps/).

rows.what: The printed Army Lists year by year, 1776 to 1815
rows.note: **Done, and it found him where three searches had not.** Four editions read in full text, free: 1783 **Second Lieutenant**, 1802 **Captain** of the Royal Engineers, 1803 Captain of the corps *and* **Major in the army**, 1821 the index carrying «D'Arcy, Lt. Col. Joseph, Royal Art.» A third printed confirmation of **17 January 1776**. The reason he had been hard to find outside: the 1783 compositor set it **D'Arcey**, with an E — a spelling this site's own search index already knew and its outside queries had never used. [The Corps](/the-corps/).

rows.what: The Manorial Documents Register for Awre, Blakeney and Berkeley
rows.note: **Done, and it found the best errand of the day.** The **Awre** court rolls survive almost unbroken and none of it is digitised: single surrenders of **1387**, 1439, 1573 and 1577/8; the rolls 1588–91; then 1671 and nearly continuous to **1881**. D3270/282 is explicitly «extracts relating to customary heir of a tenant dying», 1688–1777 and 1783–1810 — a named parent-to-child link every generation, across exactly the gap this archive cannot cross. Hamfallow and Hinton return nothing separate, and structurally cannot: they were parts of the manor of Ham, so their records are inside the Berkeley muniments.

rows.what: Read the rest of the Berkeley Castle deeds — 153 of the 178 are still unopened
rows.note: **Done, and the best single sentence of the week came out of it.** All 200 Berkeley records read for relationship language; 25 phrases tie the surname to a relationship, **six of them new**, including three generations in one Hinton lease. **BCM/A/4/2/22 of 5 December 1390** grants away «the marriage of John Swonhongre, son and heir of Elias Swonhongre, which came to Thomas because Elias held of Thomas by knight service» — confirming Smyth, explaining the wardship, and **documenting the tenure this archive had only inferred**. Five more deeds map the roads and fields, and LE WESTFELD of 1322 is the WESTFIELD of the 1601 Saniger release. [Written up](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: Transactions of the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society — 40 volumes, none read
rows.note: **Done — all 67 swept, one volume unfetchable and recorded as unread, twelve carrying the name.** Each volume controlled by its own Berkeley mention count. **Volume 22 (1899) prints the deeds in full English translation**: the 1329 indenture naming **Elyanora de Stone, mother of Alice and Joan**, which makes them sisters and explains how Wanswell came in; and the 1353 partition Smyth describes in a line, entire, keeping the Severn fishery out of the division. **Volume 10 prints a Daubeney pedigree** sourced to two royal inquisitions: John Swonhonger **aged 18 in 1393**, died 1401/2 without issue — which fits the sale of his marriage in 1390 exactly. It also corrected this archive's own «no royal inquisition» claim.

rows.what: The published Feet of Fines and Inquisitions Post Mortem for Gloucestershire
rows.note: **Done, and the fines are a dead end for a structural reason.** Gloucestershire feet of fines survive at Kew in CP 25/1 but are catalogued **only at piece level** — a county and a span of regnal years, no parties — and no free name-indexed published abstract exists. A fine naming a Swonhungre cannot be found by search. The search was not wasted: it turned up **BCM/A/1/24/189–190**, which carry the Stone line back three generations and name **Juliana** and **Elyanora**, and which turn out to be the deed Cooke called «the only foundation of the tenure of any part of the Wanswell estate».

rows.what: What the Birmingham MS 3549 collection actually is
rows.note: **Answered, and it was worth asking.** MS 3549 is **John Smyth of Nibley's own collection** — «miscellaneous deeds and manorial records collected by John Smyth», 1200–1704 — the working papers he gathered while writing the books this archive has spent a week testing. That is why the 1377 grant appears twice: he kept a copy. And the series holds **MS 3549/89, the court roll of the manor of HAM AND HINTON, 1587–88** — fourteen years before this archive's earliest Saniger deed — plus an Alkington court roll of 1624. Now errand 59.

rows.what: Why Berkeley deeds are filed in Hertfordshire
rows.note: **Answered, and the deed turned out to be much better than its snippet.** DE/M is the papers of the **Capells, Earls of Essex**; John Capel is the first party, so it travelled to Hertfordshire in his family's muniments and no Gloucestershire search could have found it. Read in full it divides «the inheritance in Hamme of **JOHN DE WYKE**» between three coheirs — **Joan Capel, Alice de Swonhongre and Agnes de Lorewynge**, each named as the ancestor her heir holds through. Alice was a coheir of John de Wyke, of the hamlet next door: **the land came into this family through a woman.**

rows.what: Edward Sanniger, mariner of Chepstow, died 1806
rows.note: **Done as far as a catalogue can take it.** Both references confirmed: **IR 26/352/152** at Kew is the Estate Duty abstract, **LL/1806/24** at the National Library of Wales is the will. Neither catalogue entry names a relative, so he remains a surname, a spelling — the same double-n as **Edward Sanniger of Berkeley, gent** in 1694 — and twenty miles of water. The NLW's own catalogue serves a **bot check**, which this archive does not complete, so the will is recorded as `blocked`, not as absent. Errand 60.

rows.what: Thomas Sanniger, Able Seaman of HMS Eurydice, will of 1794
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question; the document is an errand.** «Will of Sanniger, Thomas. Rank/Rating: Able Seaman. Ship Name: Eurydice. Ship's Pay Book number: 193», 24 February 1794, **ADM 48/84/222**. Rank, ship and pay-book number, and no kin. Seamen's wills name next of kin in the document itself, which is exactly why a catalogue search cannot settle whether he belongs here. Errand 61.

rows.what: The Swonhungre with two shops in Bristol market, 1443
rows.note: **P/St.P and J/D/2(j)** at Bristol Archives: Thomas Dodde of Stapleton, Richard Venables and **John Swonhungre**, two shops with gardens in the Market. Smyth's country line failed in 1401; this is a man of the name in a Bristol parish forty years later, in trade. This archive's later Sanigers reach Bristol too. The join is not made and should be tested rather than assumed.

rows.what: The Tudor subsidy rolls for Berkeley and Bledisloe hundreds, 1523–25
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question, and the Forest side is the part that matters.** Six pieces for **Berkeley hundred** (1543–49) and six for **BLEDISLOE** (1523–25 and 1544), every one described as «Assessment (**individuals**)» — named taxpayers. None digitised; no free published edition exists, and the Gloucestershire Record Series editions are in copyright. Bledisloe is the find: Awre and Blakeney have **no FreeREG coverage, no Protestation return and no surviving 1381 poll tax membrane**, so the subsidy and the court rolls are the only dense named sources that parish has. Errand 63.

rows.what: The poll tax of 1678, transcribed and sitting in Gloucester
rows.note: **D5555/2/14** at Gloucestershire Archives, «Poll tax return for the hundreds of Deerhurst, Cleeve and lower Westminster» — the wrong hundreds, but the same collection's **D5555/2/9** transcribes *Men and Armour* 1608, the hearth taxes of 1664 and 1672 and the poll tax of 1678 together. Establish which hundreds the 1678 return covers before adding it to an errand.

rows.what: Follow the Thorps, who took the estate in 1401
rows.note: Rudder gives them a named tower at Berkeley Castle and carries them to 1525; Smyth says the estate stayed in the name for two hundred years until George Thorpe, «his improvident…». The Thorps are the thread between the medieval hamlet and the Berkeley estate deeds of 1601 onwards, and following them is the cheapest test of whether the two Saniger groups are one family or two.

rows.what: Kane's List of Officers of the Royal Regiment of Artillery
rows.note: **Done as far as the digitised scans allow, and it confirmed a pattern.** The index to Askwith's 1900 edition of Kane's List carries exactly two D'Arcys in the Royal Artillery — **«D'Arcy, C, 16» and «D'Arcy, J., 25»** — mirroring Connolly's exactly two in the Engineers. The volumes digitised on the Internet Archive are the **biographical-notice volumes and their index**; the pages the index points at are not in these scans. Controlled: the 1869 Kane scan has «Lieutenant» only 7 times and no Shrapnel, so it is a fragment, not a null.

rows.what: The rest of the Army List run, 1776 to 1815
rows.note: Four editions were read on 15 September out of roughly forty. The four gave Second Lieutenant 1783, Captain 1802, Major 1803 — three points and a line drawn between them again, just a shorter line. The run would give a position per year and independently date the Minorca, Copenhagen and Walcheren postings Porter asserts. The method is now scripted and each volume takes about a minute.

rows.what: Constantine D'Arcy, the only other D'Arcy in Connolly's Roll
rows.note: Connolly carries exactly two D'Arcys across 1660–1898 and the second is Robert's son. His Barbados christenings are already on the site; his own career is not. He is also the one man whose record might name his father in a way his father's never did — a son's papers sometimes say what a father's omit.

rows.what: Rudder and Bigland on AWRE and BLAKENEY, not just Berkeley
rows.note: **Done, and the two authorities split cleanly.** Rudder covers the Forest parishes well — Awre 194 mentions, Blakeney 20 — and carries **no Saniger anywhere in the book**, which was already established against an 804-mention Berkeley control. Bigland gives **twenty**, and his Berkeley monuments turn out to record one household across four generations with ages: Edward Saniger gent buried 1739 **aged 48**, Susanna his relict 1744 **aged 58**, Jane their daughter 1750 **aged 24**. Plus an Edward Saniger **of Peddington** — the hamlet named beside Swanhanger in the 1626 inquisition.

rows.what: Trade directories — Pigot's and Kelly's, Gloucestershire and Staffordshire
rows.note: Free, digitised, and they list tradesmen by town with occupation. The Sanigers were weavers, clothiers and fullers; **James Sneyd was an engraver at Hanley** and his sons after him. Directories sit exactly between the censuses and would place households in years no census covers.

rows.what: Poor law settlement examinations and removal orders for Berkeley
rows.note: The record that names a labourer's parents, birthplace and marriage in one sworn document, generated for precisely the people who leave nothing else. The 1608 muster puts Sanigers at the bottom of the Vale's social scale — labourers and weavers of «lower stature» — which is the class the settlement papers exist to describe. A Discovery catalogue question first.

rows.what: Backfill the 59 nulls that name no control
rows.note: **Done, and it corrected me rather than the rows.** Reading the grandfathered list properly showed my detector was wrong in both directions: it demanded a digit, so it missed «returns **TWO** entries», «transcribed in full — 7,967 records» and «Dursley runs to 1951… so the window is **well covered**»; widening it then accepted «1841 entries», where the number is a year. **The true count is 55 named and 39 unstated of 94**, not 30 and 59. The fix was to stop guessing: `ctl` is now a **field the author sets**, and the pattern survives only as the bootstrap that set it once.

rows.what: Make the build refuse a new null that names no control
rows.note: **Done, and control-tested three ways.** `tools/check_controls.py` refuses a null with no `ctl` field, an `unstated` row that is not grandfathered, and a `ctl` on a row that is not a null — all three proved by adding bad rows and watching it exit 1. The **39 rows marked `unstated` are grandfathered by name** in `tools/controls-grandfathered.json` — they are not wrong, they are untested, each is marked «no control stated» on [/searched](/searched/), and clearing them is item 47. Proved it refuses by adding a bad row: two FAIL lines and exit 1. It runs in `build.sh` before the link check. **55 nulls currently name a control.**

rows.what: Teach agree.py to suppress the adjacent-event false positive
rows.note: **Done — 31 pairs down to 14, and the remainder are almost all the repeated-forename class the docstring already names.** Three changes, none of them «tighten the window»: a year goes to **one** event instead of every event nearby; the event word **before** the year wins, because English dates itself after naming itself; and `married` now matches «m. », which `born` and `died` already matched — the omission was why this archive's own pedigree tables read as contradictions. The **meta-registers joined SKIP**: my own note explaining the Joseph D'Arcy false positive had become a fresh source for it.

rows.what: Check that the sources this archive cites still resolve
rows.note: `check_links.py` tests internal links only. The archive now cites Internet Archive identifiers, Discovery references, Gazette issue numbers and coaley.net — all external, none tested, and a dead citation is indistinguishable from a good one on the page. A periodic external check that reports rather than gates.

rows.what: Put the medieval material on the atlas and the timeline
rows.note: Nine hundred years of the name landed on one page and nowhere else. [The timeline](/timeline/) already runs 1189–2010 and should carry the 1270s surname formation, the 1322 charter, the 1356 pedigree deed and the 1401 failure of the line. [The atlas](/atlas/) has no point for **Swonhunger** — a place on the king's highway from Longbridge, named in deeds from the mid-13th century.

rows.what: Give the medieval people dossiers, or decide deliberately not to
rows.note: The archive's `dossiers.json` and `provenance.json` carry a page per named person. Fifteen or so Swonhungres now have documented appearances — Thomas son of Thomas de Esshelesworth, William brother and heir of Thomas of Wanswell, Elias, Alice, Isabella, John the elder. Either they enter the register as people, or the archive states on the page why a 14th-century deed witness is not one. **Both answers are defensible; drifting between them is not.**

rows.what: Say on /method what a calendar is
rows.note: Everything published on 15 September rests on **modern archivists' calendars of medieval deeds**, not on the deeds. The pages say so individually. The method page does not yet name this as a grade of evidence, and it sits somewhere between `documented` and `inferred`: a competent reading by somebody who had the original, which is excellent, and is still not the document.

rows.what: Ask the Falco session whether the Bristol Swonhungre touches their Bristol material
rows.note: Cross-archive, raised here because it would otherwise go unsaid. A John Swonhungre held two shops in Bristol Market in 1443, and this estate has more than one archive with Bristol connections. Worth one question before this archive spends effort proving a link that another session has already ruled out.

rows.what: Find the 1774 conveyance Cooke describes, and settle the bridge properly
rows.note: Cooke's sentence — «Saniger Farm… was sold by **Edward Saniger to the Earl of Berkeley in 1774**» — is the join this archive has said all week it could not make, and it is currently graded **inferred** because it is a scholar's conclusion rather than a chain of deeds. The Berkeley estate papers at Gloucestershire Archives already hold Edward Saniger's mortgages of 1692, 1709 and 1716; the 1774 conveyance should be among them. Errand 62, and the most valuable single document now named anywhere on this site.
